title: Boundless compassion
hookLine: the second of the four boundless states in Buddhism

cards: An ambulance goes by with its siren on. Traffic pulls over. For a few seconds, a whole street of strangers knows that someone ahead is having one of the worst days of their life.
Some drivers say a quiet word for whoever it is. Some just feel a tug in the chest, and then the light turns green. That tug has a name in Buddhism.
Yesterday's love wished beings well; today's turns toward the ones who are hurting. It's the second of four states Buddhists call boundless.

teach.b: Buddhist texts name four qualities a person can grow until they reach every being: loving-kindness, compassion, gladness for others, and equanimity.
In the suttas, a meditator fills the world with each one in turn, one direction after another, until the whole world is covered. Karuna, compassion, is the second.

teach.h: THE WISH FOR SUFFERING TO LIFT.
teach.b: It's the wish for someone to be free of their suffering. Not fixing them, not solving them: wishing, with the whole heart, that the pain would lift.

teach.h: A FAR ENEMY AND A NEAR ONE.
teach.b: Buddhaghosa, a Buddhist teacher, says in his manual the Path of Purification that compassion has a far enemy and a near one. The far enemy is plain: cruelty.
The near enemy is sneakier, a sorrow that looks like compassion but sinks into its own grief, until the feeling is mostly about the one who feels it. Compassion stays turned toward the other person.
Where to start? Not with everyone.

Buddhaghosa says begin with one person you've seen in real misfortune, and let the wish grow: to someone dear, to someone you barely notice, and at last to someone you find hard. Boundless doesn't start boundless.

how: In Buddhist practice, compassion (karuna) is one of the four boundless states; Buddhaghosa's manual advises beginning by wishing one suffering person free of pain, then widening the wish step by step to all beings.

o: pity that looks down on someone in trouble
sadness you feel about your own losses
compassion: wishing someone's suffering would lift

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the wish for suffering to lift
a sorrow that sinks into itself

s: karuna is the wish for their suffering to lift, not a repair job.
Buddhaghosa says compassion has a near enemy that looks like it
a sorrow that sinks into its own grief instead of staying turned toward the other.
karuna is the first of the four boundless states

games.q: you want to practice compassion for the first time. by Buddhaghosa's advice, who do you start with?
o: everyone in the world at once.
one person you've seen in real misfortune.
games.why: he says begin with one person in misfortune, then widen to someone dear, someone neutral, and someone hard.

practice: Bring to mind one person who is suffering right now, someone sick, someone grieving, someone you saw on the street, and keep their face before you.

Breathing in, notice their trouble without adding to it; breathing out, wish them free of it, in words as simple as may this lift, and if the feeling turns into your own heaviness, come back to their face.
If you pray, you can hold them in a prayer from your own tradition.

wordCard.voice: Karuna. Compassion: the wish for one who suffers to be free of it, the second of the four boundless states. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: compassion, the second of the four boundless states.

carryVoice: Your line: compassion. That ends a week of love in many voices: Ibn Arabi, Mirabai, Radha, the Gita, the Sikh hymn, the Metta Sutta, and now karuna. A week well walked.

sources.ref: Tevijja Sutta (Digha Nikaya 13), the four boundless states
